title: Photonic fusion operations transform partial distinguishability
authors: S. N. van den Hoven, G. B. Lamers, J. J. Renema
abstract: Photonic fusion operations are a central primitive in photonic quantum information processing and are commonly characterized by their success probability and resource cost. Here, we identify an additional way in which different implementations of fusion operations differ, namely in how they transform partial distinguishability. We consider distinguishability originating both from imperfect entangled resource states and from imperfect single photons. We find that different successful fusion events can induce markedly different distinguishability transformations depending on the fusion protocol, heralding outcome, and error model. Under a collective resource-state error model, we identify a modification to an existing fusion protocol that improves the fidelity of the remaining state on average. Generally, however, these transformations adversely affect distinguishability, and many successful fusion outcomes are accompanied by distinguishability degradation. Our results show that partial distinguishability is dynamically shaped by interference and measurements and should be considered alongside overall fusion success probability when evaluating photonic fusion protocols.
summary: This work establishes that photonic fusion operations not only determine success rates but also dynamically shape the partial distinguishability of the resulting quantum state. By analyzing this transformation, the authors show that protocols optimized for fidelity or success might fail to account for detrimental changes in distinguishability. This mandates that distinguishability propagation be a core metric in designing robust photonic quantum circuits.
main_problem: The paper investigates a novel characterization of photonic fusion operations: how they dynamically transform partial distinguishability, moving beyond simple metrics like success probability or resource cost.
main_result: Different fusion protocols induce markedly different transformations in partial distinguishability, meaning this property must be considered alongside success probability when evaluating quantum protocols.
method: The authors analyze various fusion protocols using theoretical models (OBB/OBBell) to track the evolution of distinguishability in heralded entangled states.
model_or_system: The system is photonic quantum information processing, focusing on photonic fusion operations (Bell measurements) applied to states suffering from partial distinguishability due to imperfect photon sources or channels.
key_observables: Partial distinguishability, fidelity of the remaining state, average error reduction factor, and success probability.
important_parameters: The distinguishability parameter ($\epsilon$), the fusion protocol used, and the heralding outcome.
main_assumptions: The analysis utilizes the Orthogonal Bad Bit (OBB) and Orthogonal Bad Bell (OBBell) models, which simplify the continuous nature of realistic mode mismatch.
figures_summary: Figures compare Bell-state infidelity ($\epsilon'$) vs. distinguishability ($\epsilon$) for various protocols, and compare success probability with error reduction factors for modified protocols.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the problem of characterizing fusion operations beyond success probability, develops error models (OBB/OBBell), analyzes multiple protocols by tracking distinguishability transformation, and concludes that this dynamic property must be accounted for.
why_interesting: It provides a rigorous, quantitative framework for assessing the quality of quantum operations in photonic systems by tracking the evolution of coherence/indistinguishability, which is crucial for scaling up quantum networks.

Figure 2. Both the success probability (top) and the expectation value of the error reduction factor (bottom) are shown for var- ious fusion protocols. On the left of the bottom histogram we see that existing protocols for fusions (up to 6-photon ancillary states) all show error reduction factors below one and hence perform anti-distillation on average, while the altered Grice protocols on the right excel in terms of distillation properties. This comes at the expense of reducing the success probability.

Figure 3. For various fusion protocols, the cumulative success probability is shown as a function of a desired minimum error reduction factor. The curves therefore indicate the probability of obtaining a successful herald outcome conditioned on de- manding at least a specified degree of indistinguishability dis- tillation.
Figure 4. Comparison of the average error reduction factor for the collective distinguishability model (orange) and Bell states generated from OBB single photons (green).

Figure 5. Average fidelity of a 4-GHZ state as a function of the number of successful fusion operations for the various fusion protocols considered. All states (including ancilla states) are generated from OBB single photons. For most data points, the error bars are smaller than the markers.
